newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Shares outperform other Australia investments - ANZ.
newsitem.headline: Shares outperform other Australia investments - ANZ.

text.p: Shares outperformed other major asset classes during the June quarter and over the medium-term, Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd said in its latest quarterly ANZ Investment monitor publication.
In the year to June, the Australian and international sharemarkets rose strongly, providing returns of 26.6 percent and 29.1 percent (in Australian dollar terms) respectively.
Fixed interest also performed well, reutrning 16.8 percent.
Cash investments returned 6.1 percent, while gold continued its downward trend, falling 7.8 percent, the bank.

ANZ Funds Managements chief investment officer Glenn Woolley said in a statement the continued strong performance of investment markets was reflected in superannuation funds, which delivered an after-tax return of 17.7 percent over the past year.

Average returns for residential property over the past year were 18.2 percent, primarily due to the performance of the Sydney and Melbourne markets, which rose 30 percent and 14.9 percent respectively.
However, both markets fell during the June quarter, Sydney by 4.8 percent and Melbourne 2.6 percent respectively.

Over the past five years, shares continued to provide the best investment returns, the bank said, with Australian shares returning 15.1 percent a year, and international shares returning 16.2 percent.
Fixed interest investments returned 9.4 percent, residential property 9.8 percent and cash 6.4 percent, while gold fell 0.6 percent.

Over the ten year period, residential property returned an average of 14.1 percent a year, fixed interest 12.8 percent, cash and international shares both returned 9.5 percent, while Australian shares returned 9.1 percent.
"The latest results highlight the wisdom of holding a diversified investment portfolio to build wealth over time," Woolley said.
However, Woolley said world equity markets are well overdue for a correction, as on most valuation in general, they are over-valued.
"Investor optimism has driven the U.S. equity market to double over 30 months. These sorts of returns cannot be sustained in the medium term," he said.
